paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Quantum cryptography means using the rules of quantum mechanics to carry out the work of encryption. It draws on properties such as entanglement, superposition, the disturbance caused by measuring something, and the no-cloning theorem. Its best-known and most developed use is quantum key distribution, or QKD. In QKD, two parties, usually called Alice and Bob, build a shared secret key through quantum communication, and an eavesdropper called Eve learns nothing about it even if she listens to everything they send.

paragraphs.heading: The problem it solves
paragraphs.text: Scrambling a message is well understood; the hard part is getting the same secret key safely to both ends, a task called key establishment or key agreement. QKD is aimed squarely at that task. Once Alice and Bob hold the key, they normally use it with ordinary classical encryption, such as a one-time pad.

paragraphs.heading: Why reading it leaves a trace
paragraphs.text: Data held in a quantum state cannot be copied with perfect accuracy; this is the no-cloning theorem. Trying to read that data also changes the quantum state, through what physicists call wave function collapse. So if Eve tries to learn the key, mismatches appear and Alice and Bob notice them. The same effect can expose snooping on quantum communication links and networks.

paragraphs.heading: How strong the security is
paragraphs.text: The safety of QKD can be proven mathematically without placing any limit on what an eavesdropper is able to do, which classical key sharing cannot match. This is often called unconditional security, yet it still rests on a few assumptions. Quantum mechanics must hold, and Alice and Bob must be able to confirm each other's identity, or Eve could pose as one of them and sit in the middle.

paragraphs.heading: Secrets that must last
paragraphs.text: Nobody can assume an encryption key stays safe forever, and classical methods cannot promise protection much past about 30 years. Quantum key distribution can guard electronic records for as long as 100 years. That matters in health care, where the law requires medical records to stay secret. It also matters to governments, which have kept military data hidden for more than 60 years.

paragraphs.heading: Long, noisy lines
paragraphs.text: Studies have shown that QKD can remain secure even when sent a long way over a noisy channel. Quantum repeaters help with this. They are quantum computers placed along the line in segments, and they purify each stretch before joining the stretches into one secure connection.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: Stephen Wiesner, who was at Columbia University in the early 1970s, proposed a scheme he called conjugate coding. The IEEE Information Theory Society rejected his paper, and it finally appeared in SIGACT News in 1983. It showed how two messages could be stored in two paired properties of photons, such as linear and circular polarization, so that a receiver could decode one but never both. In 1991 Artur Ekert, working on his own, suggested using Bell's inequalities for secure key sharing.

paragraphs.heading: From theory to products
paragraphs.text: Several companies make quantum cryptography systems, among them ID Quantique in Geneva, Toshiba in Tokyo and QuintessenceLabs in Canberra. Quantum authentication is also seen as a vital part of a future quantum internet, keeping digital communication private and intact over the long run.
